overview.body:
**Dangun** (*dangun*) ​— Founder ‌of Korea, ‌First King ​· Lord ​of the ​sandalwood — belongs ​to the ​Korean tradition, ‌where it ​is catalogued ​under the domain ‌"Founder of ​Korea, First ‌King". The ​name means ‌"Lord of ​the sandalwood"[^1].

**Dangun** ​is the ​legendary founder ​of Gojoseon ​and the ‌first ancestor of ​the Korean ‌people in ​Korean tradition. ‌The name ​means "Lord ‌of the sandalwood" ​and belongs ‌to the ​domain "Founder ​of Korea, ‌First King." Dangun ‌is the ‌son of ​Hwanung, the ​heavenly prince ‌who descended ​to earth, and ​Ungnyeo, a ‌bear who ​became a ​woman after ‌enduring one hundred ​days in ‌a cave ​eating garlic ​and mugwort. ​He is ​said to have ‌founded the ‌state of ​Gojoseon at ‌Asadal in ​2333 BCE, an ​event commemorated ‌on National ‌Foundation Day, ‌3 October.[^2]

‌PuniCodex restores ​the name as ‌**Dangun** and ​serves its ​temple at ​[its temple](https://punicodex.com/dangun/). ‌The restoration needs ​no distinctive ​letters or ​diacritics its ‌ASCII form ​would lose, ​which places the ​name in ‌Tier 2. ​The plain ‌ASCII form ​*dangun* survives as ‌a modern ​convenience imposed ‌by the ‌early domain-name ​system; the ​restoration, not the ​fallback, is ​the form ‌the project ‌defends as ​philologically complete[^3].

sources.citation: Iryeon, Samguk Yusa (Memorabilia of the Three Kingdoms), 1281; English trans. Ha Tae-Hung and Grafton K. Mintz (1972).
Kim Pusik, Samguk Sagi (History of the Three Kingdoms), 1145.
Lee, Peter H., ed., Sourcebook of Korean Civilization, vol. 1 (Columbia University Press, 1993).

the-name.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in ​Hangul + ​Hanja ​as ​**단군 (檀君)**. ​Etymologically ‌it ​means "Lord ​of ‌the sandalwood"[^1].

​The ‌ASCII ​form *dangun* ‌survives ​only ​because the ​early ​domain-name ​system could ‌not ​carry diacritics; ‌it ​is ‌a technological ​compromise, ‌not ​an ancient ‌spelling. ​The ​Unicode restoration ‌**Dangun** ‌recovers the ‌full ​diacritic ​detail of ‌the ​scholarly ​transliteration directly ‌in ​the ​address bar. ‌The ​restoration needs ‌no ​distinctive ​letters or ​diacritics ​its ‌ASCII form ‌would ​lose, ‌which places ​the ​name in ‌Tier ‌2.

‌The letter-by-letter ‌transformation ​runs:

‌- **d** ​→ ​**D** ​— Same, ‌capitalized
​- **a** ​→ ​**a** ‌— Same
​- ​**n** ​→ **n** ‌— ​Same
‌- **g** ​→ ‌**g** — ​Same
‌- ‌**u** → ​**u** ​— ​Same
- ​**n** ‌→ ‌**n** — ​Same

sources.citation: Iryeon, Samguk Yusa (Memorabilia of the Three Kingdoms), 1281; English trans. Ha Tae-Hung and Grafton K. Mintz (1972).

pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed pronunciation ‌of the ‌name is ​**/taŋ.ɡun/** — ​Korean Reconstruction.[^1]

​Phoneme by ​phoneme:

​- **taŋ** ‌— The ​first syllable ​of Dangun, ‌carrying primary ​stress in ‌the ​romanised form.
‌- **ɡun** ​— The ​middle syllable ​or element, ​pronounced ​with level ‌pitch in ​Korean.
- ‌**-** — ​The final ‌syllable, often ​closing ‌in a ​nasal or ‌simple vowel ​in the ​Korean reading.

‌For the ‌modern ‌speaker, the ​closest approximation ​is: 'TAHNG-goon' ‌— The ​initial consonant ​is an ‌unaspirated ​velar stop, ​closer to ‌a soft ​‘t’ than ‌to English ​‘d’; ​the final ​nasal closes ​the first ‌syllable. The ‌scholarly capital ​marks the ‌name ​as a ​proper noun.

‌Kindred and ‌historical forms ‌of the ‌name:

- ​**Hangul** ‌— 단군 ​— the ​Korean script ​form.
- ‌**Hanja** — ​檀君 — ​the ​Sino-Korean character ‌form.

The ​initial consonant ​is an ​unaspirated velar ‌stop, ​closer to ‌a soft ​‘t’ than ‌to English ​‘d’; the ‌final nasal ‌closes ​the first ​syllable. The ​scholarly capital ​marks the ‌name as ‌a proper ​noun.

sources.citation: Iryeon, Samguk Yusa (Memorabilia of the Three Kingdoms), 1281; English trans. Ha Tae-Hung and Grafton K. Mintz (1972).

original-script.body:
The ​name is ‌preserved ‌in Hangul ​+ ​Hanja as ​**단군 ​(檀君)** — ​Korean ‌alphabet + ​Chinese ​characters, ‌attested Modern ​Korean ‌(name attested ​in ‌the Samguk ​Yusa, ​13th c.), ​in ​Korea. The ​script ‌is written ​left-to-right.[^1]

‌The scholarly ​transliteration ‌is *Dangun* ​(Revised ‌Romanization), giving ​the ‌normalized reading ​/dan.ɡun/.

​The rendering ‌proceeds ‌step ‌by step:

​- ​Hangul 단군 ‌with ​Hanja 檀君 ​— ‌the founder's ​name ​as recorded ‌in ​the Samguk ‌Yusa

​Korean names ​may ​be written ​in ‌Hangul, the ‌indigenous ​Korean alphabet, ‌and ​sometimes ​in Hanja, ‌the ‌Sino-Korean character ‌set. ‌For **Dangun**, ​the ‌Hangul form ​is ​**단군** and ​the ‌Hanja form ​is ​**檀君**. Hangul ​‘단군’ ‌and Hanja ​‘檀君’, ​attested in ​the ‌Samguk Yusa ​and ‌Samguk Sagi. ​The ‌ASCII ​form *dangun* ‌is ‌a technological ​compromise; ​the capitalised ​restoration ​**Dangun** is ‌the ‌scholarly citation ​form.

domains.body:
**Dangun** ​is the ‌legendary founder ‌of Gojoseon ​and the ​first ancestor ​of ​the Korean ​people in ‌Korean tradition. ​The name ​means "Lord ‌of the ​sandalwood" ‌and belongs ​to the ‌domain "Founder ​of Korea, ​First King." ​Dangun ​is the ​son of ‌Hwanung, the ​heavenly prince ‌who descended ​to ‌earth, and ​Ungnyeo, a ‌bear who ​became a ‌woman after ​enduring ​one hundred ‌days in ‌a cave ‌eating garlic ​and mugwort. ​He is ‌said ​to have ​founded the ‌state of ​Gojoseon at ​Asadal in ‌2333 ​BCE, an ‌event commemorated ​on National ​Foundation Day, ​3 October.[^1]

​### ‌Founder of ‌Gojoseon

Dangun ​is the ‌mythic first ​king whose ​reign marks ‌the ‌beginning of ‌Korean statehood.

‌### Son ​of Hwanung ‌and Ungnyeo

​His ​birth unites ​heavenly descent ‌with the ​transformed earth-animal, ​modelling cosmic ​and ‌terrestrial harmony.

​### Asadal

​The sacred ​capital where ‌Dangun established ​law, ‌agriculture, and ​the ordering ‌of the ​people.

### ‌Sansin

After ‌his long ​reign ​Dangun became ​a mountain ​spirit, still ‌invoked for ‌protection and ​prosperity.

sources.citation: Kim Pusik, Samguk Sagi (History of the Three Kingdoms), 1145.

symbols.body:
The ​iconography ‌associated ‌with ​Dangun concentrates ​in ​a ​small ​set ‌of ​recurring ​attributes, ‌each a ​compressed ‌statement ​about ‌the ​name:[^1]

​- ​**The ​sandalwood tree** ​— ‌Dang ​檀 ‌means ​sandalwood; ‌the ​tree ‌marks the ​sacred ‌descent ​place ​of ‌Hwanung.
‌- ‌**Bear ​and tiger** ​— ‌The ​two ​animals ‌who ​underwent ​Hwanung's ‌trial; the ​bear's ‌perseverance ​became ​the ​origin ​of ‌the ‌Korean people.
​- ‌**Garlic ​and ​mugwort** ‌— ‌The ‌austere ‌foods of ​transformation, ‌marking ​the ​passage ​from ‌animal ​to ​human and ​from ‌wilderness ​to ​culture.
​- ‌**Mountain ​peak** ‌— The ​place ‌where ​Dangun ‌withdrew ‌and ​continues ​to ​dwell as ​a ‌protective ‌mountain ​spirit.

sources.citation: Iryeon, Samguk Yusa (Memorabilia of the Three Kingdoms), 1281; English trans. Ha Tae-Hung and Grafton K. Mintz (1972).

mythology.body:
The mythology ​of Dangun ‌is preserved ‌in Korean ​oral tradition, ​shamanic ritual ​texts, and ​classical sources ​such as ‌the Samguk ​Yusa. The ​narratives are ‌not merely ​stories; they encode ‌social values, ​ritual obligations, ‌and relationships ​between humans, ​nature, and ​the sacred. ​Some details ​vary by ‌region and ​by shamanic ‌lineage.[^1]

### ​The Bear and ‌the Tiger ​(Samguk Yusa)

‌Hwanung tested ​a bear ‌and a ​tiger by ​locking them ‌in a ‌cave with ‌only garlic ​and mugwort. ​The tiger ‌gave up, but ​the bear ​endured one ‌hundred days ​and became ​a woman ‌named Ungnyeo. ​Hwanung then ‌took her ​as his ​wife, and ​she bore ​Dangun.[^2]

### The ‌Founding of ‌Gojoseon (Foundation ​myth)

Dangun ‌established the ​capital at ​Asadal and ‌ruled over ‌Gojoseon for ‌one thousand ‌five hundred ​years. The ‌date traditionally ​given for the ​founding, 3 ​October 2333 ‌BCE, is ​celebrated as ​National Foundation ​Day.

### ‌Dangun Becomes ​Mountain Spirit ​(Apotheosis)

At ​the end ‌of his ​reign Dangun left ‌the affairs ​of state ‌and withdrew ​into the ‌mountains, where ‌he became ​a sansin, ​a mountain ​deity who ​continues to ‌protect the ‌land and ​its people.

archaeology.body:
No ​monument, ‌inscription, or ‌artifact ​in ​the ​current ​PuniCodex corpus ​is ‌yet ​assigned ​to ‌Dangun with ​certainty. ‌That ​absence ‌should be ​read ​honestly: ​for ​a ​Korean name ‌of ​this ‌type ​the material ‌record ​is ‌expected ​to ‌be thin, ​and ​the ‌primary ‌evidence ‌remains the ​textual ​testimony ‌gathered ​in the ​Scholarly ‌Sources ​section[^1].

​Were ‌such evidence ​to ‌surface, ​it ​would ​take recognizable ​forms: ‌votive ‌or ​dedicatory inscriptions ‌naming ​단군 ​(檀君), ‌sanctuary ‌or cult ‌remains ‌tied ​to ‌founder ​of korea ​and ​iconography ‌matching ​its traditional ​attributes ​(the ‌sandalwood ​tree ​and bear ​and ‌tiger). ​Each ‌candidate would ​be ‌weighed ​against ‌the ‌reconstructed form ​of ​the ​name ​before ‌entering the ‌scholarly ​record.

sources.citation: Iryeon, Samguk Yusa (Memorabilia of the Three Kingdoms), 1281; English trans. Ha Tae-Hung and Grafton K. Mintz (1972).
